reasons_add: Sībawayh says sung rhyme prolongs endings with alif, yāʾ or wāw, with or without tanwīn, matching the preceding vowel because poetry is made for singing; he illustrates different inflections with lines of Imruʾ al-Qays (manzilī), Yazīd ibn al-Thaʿthariyya (maṣraʿā), al-Aʿshā (lāʾimū) and Jarīr (al-ʿitābā, al-khiyāmū, al-ayyāmā). He reports that Hijaz reciters retain these endings even without melody to mark verse, many Tamīmīs replace the length letter with nūn, as in al-ʿAjjāj's al-dharfan and annahajan, and a third practice drops prolongation, as in Jarīr's al-ʿitāb and al-Akhṭal's faʿal. When the preceding consonant is the rhyme, final yāʾ and wāw may be treated like appended length letters and even a weak radical may be omitted; al-Khalīl distinguishes yāʾ and wāw retained as the rhyme letter itself in yaqḍī and yaghzū, as qāf is in his cited line. Sībawayh says alif remains in yakhshā and yarḍā as in ordinary speech, unlike deletable yāʾ; al-Khalīl cites poetry retaining the alif of ṭayrā like taqaḍḍā and deleting the wāw of taqaddamū. Sībawayh says many of Qays and Asad even omit pronominal yāʾ and wāw, less often because they convey noun meaning; he cites omitted plural endings in ṣanaʿ, qanaʿ, jamaʿ and Ibn Muqbil's awjaf, and feminine endings in ʿAntara's takallam and al-Khazzāz ibn Lawdhān's idhhab, while the hāʾ in shattā ṭarāʾiquhu is retained because it is not a weak or length letter. He explains that a still or jussive rhyme ending can be moved and lengthened as poetic license, requiring kasra in genitive rhyme lest nominative or accusative rhyme be iqwāʾ; lines of Imruʾ al-Qays and Ṭarafa and Abū al-Najm's rajaz ending in ḥulī and maskanah illustrate this. In ordinary hesitation, Sībawayh adds examples of lengthening a final vowel (qālā, yaqūlū, al-ʿām) and using kasra on a final consonant (qadī, alī, sayfnī) to keep speech open while recollecting.
